references.text: The immediate context: Jesus meets the sick man at the Pool of Bethesda and commands him to stand up, take his mat, and walk ([ref:Joh 5:5-8|John 5:5-8]). Verse 9 describes the instantaneous healing in response to Jesus' words.
The Jews react to the man carrying his mat on the Sabbath ([ref:Joh 5:10-12|John 5:10-12]). Verse 9b sets up this Sabbath conflict by noting that the healing took place on a Sabbath.

The Sabbath conflict escalates: The Jews persecute Jesus because he healed on the Sabbath, and Jesus responds by calling God his Father ([ref:Joh 5:16-18|John 5:16-18]). This shows the theological significance of the Sabbath note in verse 9.

The healing of the man born blind also took place on a Sabbath, leading to similar conflicts between Jesus and the Pharisees ([ref:Joh 9:14-16|John 9:14-16]). The parallel reveals a recurring pattern in the Gospel of John.
The Sabbath commandment in the Ten Commandments forbids work on the Sabbath ([ref:2 Mos 20:8-11|Exodus 20:8-11]). This is the commandment the Jews believed was broken when the man carried his mat.

Jeremiah conveys the Lord's prohibition against carrying burdens on the Sabbath day ([ref:Jer 17:21-22|Jeremiah 17:21-22]). This prophetic text likely underlies the Jewish objection to the man carrying his mat.
Nehemiah rebukes those who carry burdens on the Sabbath ([ref:Neh 13:15-19|Nehemiah 13:15-19]). This illustrates the Old Testament background for the Sabbath prohibition against carrying things.
In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus heals the paralytic and says, "Stand up, take your mat and go home" ([ref:Mark 2:11-12|Mark 2:11-12]). The same kind of command and immediate healing as in John 5.
Jesus heals a woman who had been bent over on the Sabbath, which arouses the anger of the synagogue leader ([ref:Luk 13:10-14|Luke 13:10-14]). Here too, healing and Sabbath conflict are central.
Peter heals the lame man at the Beautiful Gate in Jesus' name, and the man "sprang up and began to walk" ([ref:Apg 3:6-8|Acts 3:6-8]). The parallel with the immediate, complete healing is clear.

Peter heals Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years, and says, "Stand up and make your bed!" ([ref:Apg 9:33-34|Acts 9:33-34]). The pattern of long-term illness and instantaneous healing recalls John 5:5-9.

Jesus heals the man with the withered hand on the Sabbath and defends it by saying that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath ([ref:Matt 12:10-12|Matthew 12:10-12]). The same kind of Sabbath conflict as in John 5.
